paperTitle: Deep Learning for Pixel Art Sprite Generation: A Modified Pix2Pix Approach for Line Art to Grayscale and Color Translation
centralContribution: This paper proposes and evaluates a deep-learning-based asset generation technique for pixel art sprites, specifically translating line art sketches into grayscale and color sprites. The primary contribution is a modified Pix2Pix architecture, designed to assist game artists by automating the time-consuming shading and coloring steps for 2D fighting game characters, demonstrating its effectiveness through qualitative, quantitative, and character designer evaluations within the pipeline of "Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate."

units.title: Core Contribution

content.description: The paper introduces a deep-learning technique using a modified Pix2Pix architecture to automate the generation of grayscale and color pixel art sprites from line art sketches, aiming to reduce asset creation time for game developers by streamlining the shading and coloring processes.

units.conceptualOrigin: Core Contribution of Pixel Art Sprite Generation
units.whyThisUnit: This unit highlights the main research objective and achievement, serving as the central piece of the exhibit.

units.title: Paper Abstract

content.description: Game development, particularly for pixel art, faces high costs due to extensive manual asset creation. This paper addresses this by proposing a deep-learning solution for generating semi-final pixel art sprites from line art sketches, framing it as two image translation problems (line art to gray, and gray to color) using a modified Pix2Pix architecture to automate shading and coloring, thereby decreasing character development time.

units.whyThisUnit: This unit provides a concise overview of the paper's context, problem statement, and the proposed approach.

units.title: U-Net Architecture
units.summary: Overview of the modified U-Net architecture for sprite generation.

content.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the U-Net architecture. The orange colored encoder network (on the left) and the green colored decoder network (on the right) are two components linked through standard and skip connections.
content.description: Overview of the modified U-Net architecture. Features an encoder and two distinct decoder-discriminator pairs for grayscale and RGB color-space problems. This dual-objective design allows the shared encoder to learn rich features from distinct training signals.

content.caption: Figure 12: Example of color noise evidenced after the color rounding post processing. On the gray sprite, subtle noise can be seen in the sprite contour, as well as around transitions from bright to darker areas, in the arms and legs, for example. In the color sprite, the noise is very noticeable in the beak, girl, feet and tail.
content.description: Color noise artifacts after rounding post-processing, visible in both gray and color sprites due to quantization.
